summary: A report on an experiment in which Rand graphic consoles were connected over the ARPANET to UCSB's Online System. The first phase let visitors from UCSB and TRW use it from Rand, and the second phase involved cleaning up the implementation and revisiting strategy.

eli5.summary: Researchers in one city used a drawing screen to work on a computer in another city through the network. They report how it went and what they are fixing.

subtitle: A progress report on connecting Rand graphics consoles over the ARPANET to UCSB's On-Line System.

tldr.problem: The Network Graphics Meeting in July outlined experiments to explore graphics over the Network.
tldr.mechanism: Rand's Video-Graphics System consoles reached UCSB's On-Line System (OLS) through a module added to the Rand Network Services Program, with input from a tablet and function buttons on screen.
tldr.outcome: The first phase finished in August. The second phase was cleaning up the implementation and revisiting strategies, with a presentation planned for the October graphics meeting. It updates RFC 74.

today: RFC 225 updates RFC 74 and is a snapshot of a 1971 experiment. The metadata lists its status as Unknown and no later RFC as replacing it.

sections.title: The Experiment
sections.content:
After the July Network Graphics Meeting, one outlined experiment was using the UCSB On-Line System (OLS) from graphic consoles at Rand. The connection was completed in the latter half of August and used experimentally since then. OLS users from UCSB and TRW visited Rand and used OLS via Rand consoles and the Network, completing the first phase in August.

The second phase involves cleaning up the initial implementation and reviewing and modifying the initial strategies.
sections.eli5: Visitors used a faraway computer from a screen in another building and it worked.

sections.title: How It Was Built
sections.content:
UCSB had a Network interface on the OLS described in RFC 74, modified to match current Network protocols (NCP and ICP) and a general graphics description. The OLS receives an EBCDIC-like input byte stream and generates an unstructured graphical output stream.

At Rand, the Video-Graphics System (VGS) was used. VGS consoles were already connected through the Rand Network Services Program (NSP), which had been designed for NCP checkout, logging in to remote systems and use of UCSB RJE and UCLA RJS. An extra module for the OLS was easily added.
sections.eli5: Rand already had a way to reach other computers, so they just added one more piece for the drawing computer.

sections.title: The Console Screen
sections.content:
Input is by moving a tablet cursor, shown as a small dot, to a function button and pressing the pen down. The screen has a feedback line at the top, the OLS output display in the rest of the upper half, and a sensitive area of buttons in the lower half.

The sensitive areas have three classes: a right-most column (CALL, CLOSE) that connects and disconnects, plus COPY for hardcopy on an SC 4060; the grid of OLS function buttons normally on a special function keyboard; and an area for numbers, characters and punctuation. The figures show the initial display, the login sequence and SIN and COS curves from -PI to +PI.
sections.eli5: You point a pen at buttons on the screen instead of typing, like a touchscreen.

sections.title: What Comes Next
sections.content: The authors planned to present the experiment at the October graphics meeting in two forms: a description of the protocols and techniques with conclusions, and a film showing OLS used from Rand. The protocols were to be documented when experimentation was complete.
sections.eli5: They will show everyone what they learned with a talk and a movie.

references.text: RFC 74, describing the UCSB On-Line System network interface.
